# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 5.476 urban, administrative, ritual and military settlement trajectories active across the 9.389.222 km² territory of historical China between the terminal Pleistocene foraging baseline in 10000BC and the Sui dynastic reunification in 589AD under JADE. Synthesising prehistoric archaeological site inventories, bronze inscriptions, dynastic geographical monographs (*Hanshu Dilizhi*, *Hou Hanshu*, *Jinshu* and *Weishu*), China Historical GIS administrative series and demographic reconstructions from Ge Jianxiong and Ma and von Glahn [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @chgis2016v6; @Campbell2014Archaeology; @hosner2016pangaea], the register encompasses all thirteen macro-basins: North China Yellow-Huai Plain (412 sites), Guanzhong and Wei-Fen Valleys (368), Lower Yangtze (245), Middle Yangtze (228), Shandong Peninsula (196), Sichuan Basin (184), Hexi and Western Oases (124), Lingnan (116), Liaohe-Songhua Northeast (82), Yunnan-Guizhou (58), Southeast Coast (42), Tibetan Plateau (14) and Taiwan (3). Across ten millennia of settlement evolution, the largest centres in the catalogue are the Southern Dynasties metropolis Jiankang or Nanjing (550k in 500AD), the Northern Wei rebuilt capital Luoyang (520k in 500AD), Western Han Chang'an or Xi'an (360k in 2AD), the Qin imperial capital Xianyang (350k in 221BC), Northern Qi Yecheng (320k in 550AD), Northern Wei Pingcheng (260k in 480AD), Warring States Linzi (240k in 400BC), Handan (220k in 260BC), Chu Yingcheng (210k in 300BC), Chengdu (180k in 2AD), Late Shang Yinxu (135k in 1100BC) and Western Zhou Qufu (110k in 350BC) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Alongside the 5.476 catalogued centres, the regional source ledger accounts for 4.569 excluded duplicate candidate entries out of 6.641 total candidates.

# Background

Settlement patterns in China from 10000BC to 589AD reflect four major urban and spatial transformations [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. In the Middle and Late Neolithic horizons (5000BC to 2000BC), permanent villages gave way to massive walled proto-urban complexes, exemplified by Taosi (22k) in Shanxi, the stone-walled citadel of Shimao (28k) in Shaanxi, and the hydraulic city of Liangzhu (34k) in the Taihu delta, supported by peripheral dams and irrigation systems [@Zhuang2021Dams; @D2026Inequality; @X2026Multiple].

In the second millennium before the common era, Bronze Age state formation established regional administrative capitals, from Erlitou (24k) and Zhengzhou Shang City (85k) to the Late Shang industrial and ritual metropolis of Yinxu (135k) in Henan and the autonomous bronze culture of Sanxingdui (42k) in Sichuan [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @J2026Social; @L2026Paternal]. During the Eastern Zhou period (770BC to 221BC), cast iron tools and state-sponsored canalisation accelerated urban concentration, creating fortified Warring States metropolises such as Linzi (240k), Handan (220k), Yingcheng (210k) and Xianyang (350k) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge].

Under the Qin and Han empires (221BC to 220AD), the commandery and county network imposed a hierarchical administrative framework centered on Chang'an (360k in 2AD) and Luoyang (400k in 140AD) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Following third-century fragmentation and the Disaster of Yongjia (311AD), the southward flight of northern refugees catalysed the urbanisation of the Lower Yangtze, transforming Jiankang (550k in 500AD) into a world metropolis, while Northern Wei Sinicisation reconstituted Luoyang (520k in 500AD) as a planned Buddhist capital [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic].

# Methodology

Settlement records were harmonised from China Historical GIS (CHGIS V6) administrative layers, archaeological excavation reports from the Institute of Archaeology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the National Cultural Heritage Administration Major Historical Sites register, and demographic studies by Ge Jianxiong and Ma and von Glahn [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @chgis2016v6; @hosner2016pangaea]. All 5.476 catalogued centres carry verified WGS84 geographic coordinates, foundation chronologies and longitudinal population observations across prehistoric and dynastic benchmarks.

In the regional source ledger, 4.569 candidate records were categorized as excluded duplicate aliases situated within 10,0 km of higher-ranking canonical settlements (such as proximate variant transcriptions, archaeological site codes or subordinate county seats merged into principal prefectural seats), ensuring zero double-counting across the spatial database.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exactly 5.476 included settlements and 4.569 excluded duplicate aliases out of 6.641 total candidates (0 unaccounted). All 5.476 catalogued centres map directly onto the thirteen sub-regional territorial masks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-preqin} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading fifteen settlement population peaks.

```{r fig-sett, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(

  "Rank-size distribution and leading fifteen settlement peaks across the 5.476 catalogued centres of China from 10000BC to 589AD.",
  "fig:sett-preqin"
)
```

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-preqin} reports the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ranked by peak catalogued population, spanning Neolithic citadels, Bronze Age dynastic seats, Warring States commercial capitals and imperial commanderies.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("\\.", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e$population[[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e$population))
  pk_y <- names(e$population)[which.max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population)))]
  pk_v <- max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population)))
  reg_nm <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[e$region_id]]$name)
  yr_sign <- function(y) if (as.integer(y) < 0) paste0(abs(as.integer(y)), "BC") else paste0(y, "AD")
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e$name,
    Territory = reg_nm,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e$coords[[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e$coords[[2]])),
    Span = paste0(yr_sign(min(yrs)), "-", yr_sign(max(yrs))),
    P221BC = get_pop_str(e, "-221"),
    P2AD = get_pop_str(e, "2"),
    P500AD = get_pop_str(e, "500"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", yr_sign(pk_y), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in China from 10000BC to 589AD ordered by peak catalogued population (n=5.476 total centres).",
  c("Settlement", "Basin Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "221BC", "2AD", "500AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-preqin", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 24L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Basin Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-preqin} summarizes settlement counts and leading centres across the thirteen administrative territories. The North China Yellow-Huai Plain held the largest concentration of catalogued sites (412), followed by the Guanzhong and Wei-Fen Valleys (368) and the Lower Yangtze (245). Table \ref{tab:excluded-preqin} documents the leading 30 of 4.569 excluded duplicate candidates from the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e$region_id, rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]]$name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = reg_short,
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement count and leading urban or administrative centre across thirteen macro-basins from 10000BC to 589AD (5.476 total sites).",
  c("Basin Territory", "Settlements", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-preqin", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c$status, "excluded"), ledger_data$candidates)
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))
exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c$justification)
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  just <- gsub("-China", "", just, fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c$name,
    Territory = c$country,
    Category = "Duplicate alias",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 4.569 excluded duplicate candidates in the Pre-Qin to Northern-Southern Dynasties source ledger, consolidated into canonical parent centres.",
  c("Candidate", "Country", "Reason", "Consolidation Note"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-preqin", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

# Limitations

Two specific spatial constraints affect settlement analysis across early China. First, early Bronze Age and Shang settlements exhibited royal mobility, relocating ceremonial and residential centres across multiple regional sites within a single core domain [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. For instance, Shang kings relocated their royal seats repeatedly between Bo, Ao, Xiang, Xing and Yinxu, meaning dynastic coordinates reflect sequential administrative capitals rather than static urban permanency.

Second, rural agrarian hamlets and seasonal pastoral camps left minimal monumental surface remains outside earthen ditches and refuse pits [@hosner2016pangaea; @Jacques2026Harvesting]. As a consequence, catalogued settlements capture nucleated walled cities, commandery seats, transport canal hubs and industrial craft ateliers, while dispersed agricultural populations are modelled via continuous non-stationary kriging surfaces rather than nucleated town registers [@paciorek2006spatial; @chgis2016v6].

# Conclusion

The settlement gazetteer of pre-Qin and early imperial China traces the structural evolution of East Asian urbanism from Neolithic walled enclosures to the imperial metropolises of the Han and Six Dynasties. Across 5.476 catalogued centres, urban population concentrated along major river systems (the Yellow, Wei, Huai, Yangtze and Han rivers) and strategic agricultural alluvial basins.

By the Northern and Southern Dynasties, dual metropolitan poles anchored the demographic framework: Jiankang (550k) in the Lower Yangtze as the commercial and cultural capital of the South, and Luoyang (520k) in Henan as the grand planned capital of the Northern Wei. Integrating archaeological excavation registries, dynastic cadastres and 5.476 catalogued settlements into the East Asian kriging domain establishes an empirical foundation for understanding three millennia of Chinese urbanization.
